text: CASE (12MKS) bd DOUBLE L COMPANY Double L was founded in 1957 by Mary and Phil Lamount as a part time business in their garage. Their expertise lied in electrical field and the dream of making.an electrical car always seemed far fetched. Phil Jr. seemed to have his parents expertise in technical competence. It was not until their son Phil Jr. went through a certification programme did their business dream start looking realistic. Initially he started with making inexpensive kitchen appliances with alloys. By 1981, Phil Jr. employed 32 people on its production lines and another 5 who looked at administrative duties, including a marketing manager Ralph Egerton. Ralph worked with industry reps and personally performed a small amount of direct marketing. By 1984, Phil Jr. had begun tinkering with the use of alloys in the development of an engine that could be used to power a lawn mower. In 1986, Phil Jr. completed nearly 50% of the work with improved and lighter engines, with alloys that could withstand higher temperatures than conventional lawn mower engines and thus permitted improvement in the new design. 4/3 Double L’s capital was however limited and was not allowing them to produce a line of mowers. Ralph was asked to contact the largest mower manufacturer in the US, Breeze Inc. Phil Jr. might have asked Ralph to contact other manufacturers as well but he reasoned that in their oligopsonist market each producer would want to make most out of a product differentiation. Ralph had met Mary in Breeze to crack the deal, but Mary would not allow him to meet anyone else in the organization, neither would she work on schedule and honor deadlines. The pressure was rising on Ralph as Phil Jr. was always very impatient. One day Ralph reported that Mary had given them a huge opportunity of sending their new motors to Breeze for testing, which would eventually give them their BIG order. Post sending the motor, there was no communication or follow up from Mary. After interrogating Ralph was told they Breeze was more convinces by a “new motor” developed by their competitor NR Sud and would go ahead with a contract with them. Ralph suddenly felt that probably Phil Jr. had set his price too high to crack the deal. Let down by Double L, Ralph jokingly asked Mary if they had an opening for a Marketing Manager! To which she was more than willing to have him with Breeze.

text: CASE (12MKS) PRENTICE MACHINE. TOOLS Prentice was a moderate-size, regional producer of hand tools such as hammers, saws, chisels, bits etc. Competition came from a number of large national competitors, and many specialty producers. Low cost imports were a growing influence in the American market and represented about 10% of total sales. Prentice strategy had always been to price 10-15 percent below the level of top four competitors. The Co. spent almost nothing on advertising, relying instead upon price to generate sales in major retail outlets. It also had an active private-label program, which accounted for a growing 30% of its total sales. Prentice realized a tight 3% profit on sales which was a constant over the past 4 yrs despite market fluctuations. On Jan 15, 1979, one of the major competitors (no 3 brand) announced a national price program consisting of permanent price cuts of 10-25 percent at retail. Their objective seemed to buy market share. 1/2 Prentice had the following options — 1. Do nothing —which will put the firm at a major disadvantage 2. Immediately drop prices to match the competitor — which will cause severe retaliation with the competitors 3. Some combination of marketing effort — which will give the firm some breathing time. 4. Try to reduce internal cost — in order to try and match the competing prices. The firm had 6 salesmen who worked with distributors and sold a few large private accounts directly. Exclusive use of market reps would cost them typically 5% commission on direct sales.

text: CASE (12MKS) FRANK SUD FURNITURE Frank Sud Furniture (FSD) is one of the many small companies that abound in the furniture industry. The plants value is approx $15 million, and it employs 186 people in management and production. It deals in high priced and custom made furniture. It’s a small market but profitability is relatively high. Only a handful of custom manufacturers now exist. FSD has expanded 3 times since inception. Sales have traditionally been carried on by a very limited number of “ high class” outlets and company salespeople decorators. This allows FSD to have complete control over its marketing and production processes. The store works on a very small inventory which is supplemented by company catalogs. The Salesforce works through these catalogs only. The Co. also supports them with large show rooms. This is considered to be a really expensive sales structure by most furniture manufacturers. \ t/2 Mr. Sud now wants to change his marketing structure. Offers from fine furniture stores have been forthcoming regularly for years but have been rejected regularly on grounds that Mr. Sud will himself lose control. However, 2 large showrooms have requested Mr. Sud to handle their product. One, Sud showrooms of New York, with 5 showrooms on the east cost, has been increasingly persistent. It has approx. 30 decorators per showroom and one of the highest caliber showrooms in the east. Two, Knife and Tubes, has showrooms in Chicago, Dallas, LA and Denver. With 25 decorators per show room it would give FSD more coverage in large cities west of Mississippi. Both Co’s have offered to assimilate the present company sales personnel in their respective areas, and both have agreed to show substantial amount to FSD. FSD is now considering all possibilities.

text: Read the following case carefully and answer the questions that follow: In the first week of July 1996, Ashok Kumar, Marketing Manager of Star Material Handling Company Ltd (SMHC) was analysing the marketing performance of the first quarter (i.e. April 1996-June 1996) period. He was preparing himself for the performance review meeting with the Managing Director, scheduled in the second week of July 1996. Mr. Kumar was concerned to note that the orders received in the first quarter for a range of material handling equipment were Rs 3.50 crore compared to the budgeted figure of Rs 5 crore, that is, a drop of 30 per cent. When he compared the actual orders received during the same period for the previous year (i.e. April 1995-June 1995), the present order was lower by 8 per cent. Besides, receivables (debtors) from customers had gone up to 65 days from the previous quarter figure of 35 days. Mr Kumar wondered whether the unfavourable performance was due to the changes taking place in the external marketing environment, and if so, how to manage the same. The life of the equipment varied from 5 years to 15 years, depending on how the equipment was serviced and used. EXTERNAL ENVIRONMENT Mr. Kumar felt that the economic environment had changed in the past 6 months or so, after finalization of the company's budget; since there was a slowing down of investment in new projects. In the previous 2 to 3 years, due to liberalization and reforms introduced by the Government of India, many new projects came up for expansions/diversifications which helped the company to grow by about 100 per cent compound rate of growth per year. Mr. Kumar wondered whether the change in political situation, with the installation of a new coalition Government in mid-1996, had contributed to the political uncertainty and slowing down of the economic environment. Mr. Kumar also noticed that receivables from customers had gone up to 65 days from the previous quarter performance of 35 days.
